bug_categories.description: Swap only two of the four bytes, e.g. change the concatenation to { in[31:24], in[15:8], in[23:16], in[7:0] } or leave one byte pair in its original position.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a pure 32-bit endianness swap; leaving the outer or inner byte pair unswapped yields a plausible but incorrect output that only fails for specific byte positions.

bug_categories.description: Replace the concatenation with { in[31:24], in[23:16], in[15:8], in[7:0] } or assign out = in, so the module passes data through unchanged.
bug_categories.applicability: A designer forgetting the byte reordering turns the endian converter into a wire; palindromic inputs would still pass, so only asymmetric test vectors detect it.

bug_categories.description: Use the same source byte twice in the concatenation, e.g. { in[7:0], in[15:8], in[15:8], in[31:24] }, so one input byte is lost and another is duplicated.
bug_categories.applicability: The concatenation has four 8-bit slices, and a copy-paste error in one index range is a realistic mistake that silently drops information.

bug_categories.description: Shift a slice range by one bit, e.g. in[8:1] instead of in[7:0] or in[16:9] instead of in[15:8], while keeping the width at 8 bits.
bug_categories.applicability: All slices are exact 8-bit ranges with boundaries at multiples of 8; off-by-one boundaries produce shifted data that remains valid Verilog with matching width.

bug_categories.description: Reverse bit order within each byte (e.g. using { in[0],in[1],...,in[7] } style slices) or reverse the entire 32-bit word bit by bit instead of swapping bytes.
bug_categories.applicability: Confusing byte-swap with full bit-reversal is a common mistake; the output differs only in intra-byte bit order, so byte-level checks could miss it.

bug_categories.description: Change one slice width, e.g. in[6:0] instead of in[7:0] or in[15:9], so the concatenation is narrower than 32 bits and the output is zero-extended in the MSBs.
bug_categories.applicability: The 32-bit output is assigned from a concatenation of four slices; a shortened slice leads to implicit zero extension and corrupted upper bits without a syntax error.

bug_categories.bug_type: Wrong byte rotation instead of swap
bug_categories.description: Implement a byte rotation such as { in[23:16], in[15:8], in[7:0], in[31:24] } or { in[7:0], in[31:24], in[23:16], in[15:8] } instead of a full reversal.
bug_categories.applicability: A rotate and a reversal both permute the same four bytes, so a rotation looks plausible but yields the wrong ordering for every nontrivial input.

bug_categories.description: Replace one byte with a constant or mask, e.g. { in[7:0], in[15:8], in[23:16], 8'h00 } or AND a byte with 8'hF0, forcing bits to fixed values.
bug_categories.applicability: The purely combinational path means any stuck or masked byte directly corrupts the output, emulating a stuck-at fault or an incorrect masking operation on one lane.

bug_categories.description: Swap the assignment order of the concatenation so out_hi receives in[7:0] and out_lo receives in[15:8], i.e. assign {out_lo, out_hi} = in;
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a pure byte split; the concatenation order on the left-hand side determines which byte goes to which output, so reversing it is a simple, valid-Verilog change that silently swaps the bytes.

bug_categories.description: Reverse bit ordering of one or both outputs, e.g. assign out_lo = {in[0],in[1],in[2],in[3],in[4],in[5],in[6],in[7]};
bug_categories.applicability: Each output is an 8-bit slice of the 16-bit input; explicit bit-level remapping yields endianness-at-bit-level errors that preserve widths but corrupt data.

bug_categories.description: Split the input at the wrong boundary, e.g. out_hi = in[16:9] style shifts or out_hi = in[14:7] and out_lo = in[6:0] padded, so the slices are misaligned by one bit.
bug_categories.applicability: The 16-bit input is divided at bit 8; shifting the boundary by one bit makes the high and low bytes contain bits from the wrong half while still being 8 bits wide.

bug_categories.description: Make one output narrower or drive it from a truncated slice, e.g. assign out_lo = in[6:0]; leaving out_lo[7] zero-extended, or declare out_hi as [6:0].
bug_categories.applicability: The outputs must be exactly 8 bits each; truncating a slice drops the MSB of a byte, losing data while remaining syntactically valid.

bug_categories.description: Force one bit of an output to a constant, e.g. assign out_hi[7] = 1'b0; or tie out_lo[0] to 1'b1 instead of passing the input bit.
bug_categories.applicability: Combinational pass-through has no logic to mask a stuck bit, so a single bit tie-off corrupts one data bit for all input values.

bug_categories.description: Drive both outputs from the same input half, e.g. assign out_hi = in[7:0]; assign out_lo = in[7:0]; or have one bit sourced from the wrong index (out_hi[3] = in[2]).
bug_categories.applicability: Both outputs are slices of the same bus; a copy-paste style indexing error makes the upper or lower half of the input never reach any output.

bug_categories.description: Invert one or both outputs or individual bits, e.g. assign {out_hi, out_lo} = ~in; or out_hi = ~in[15:8];
bug_categories.applicability: A pass-through design should preserve polarity; inserting a bitwise NOT keeps widths valid but flips data values.

bug_categories.bug_type: Unintended logic operation on data path
bug_categories.description: Replace the direct wire with a bitwise operation mixing halves, e.g. out_lo = in[7:0] ^ in[15:8]; or out_hi = in[15:8] & in[7:0];
bug_categories.applicability: Because the module is purely combinational slicing, introducing an XOR/AND/OR between the two bytes changes functionality while remaining valid and combinational, and cross-contaminates the outputs.

mutants.bug_type: Unintended logic operation on data path

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND operator in the continuous assignment with OR (a | b), so out_assign is 1 when either input is high.
bug_categories.applicability: out_assign = a & b is the only logic on that output, so changing the operator directly alters the truth table (differs for inputs 01 and 10).

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND in the always block with XOR (a ^ b), so out_alwaysblock is high only when inputs differ and low when both are 1.
bug_categories.applicability: out_alwaysblock = a & b in the combinational always block; the change makes it diverge from out_assign on 01, 10 and 11 and breaks the intended equivalence of the two implementations.

bug_categories.description: Negate the result of the AND on one output, e.g. out_assign = ~(a & b), turning it into a NAND.
bug_categories.applicability: Both outputs are plain AND results, so adding an inversion on one of them makes it the complement of the other for all input combinations.

bug_categories.bug_type: Input inversion / missing negation on one operand
bug_categories.description: Invert one input operand in an expression, e.g. out_alwaysblock = a & ~b.
bug_categories.applicability: Only two single-bit inputs feed the logic; inverting b (or a) changes the output for 01/11 (or 10/11) while remaining syntactically valid.

bug_categories.description: Replace always @(*) with a partial sensitivity list such as always @(a), so the output doesn't update when b changes.
bug_categories.applicability: out_alwaysblock depends on both a and b; sensitivity only to a makes simulation behavior stale/latch-like after b-only transitions, mismatching out_assign.

bug_categories.description: Use the same input twice or a wrong signal, e.g. out_assign = a & a (or a & a-only), ignoring b.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has only inputs a and b; replacing b with a makes the output simply follow a, which is a subtle copy-paste style error.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical operator confusion combined with constant override
bug_categories.description: Replace the expression with a constant or stuck value, e.g. out_alwaysblock = 1'b0 or a & 1'b1, so the output is stuck-at-0 or ignores b.
bug_categories.applicability: Simple single-assignment always block makes it easy to insert a stuck-at fault or tie an operand to a constant, leaving valid Verilog with broken functionality.

bug_categories.bug_type: Blocking vs non-blocking / assignment style error leading to sequential behavior
bug_categories.description: Change the combinational always block to use a non-blocking assignment (<=) or an edge-triggered sensitivity such as always @(posedge a), making out_alwaysblock registered/clocked by a instead of combinational.
bug_categories.applicability: out_alwaysblock is declared as output reg and driven in an always block, so converting it to edge-triggered behavior is valid Verilog and makes it lag or miss changes compared to out_assign.

mutants.bug_type: Input inversion / missing negation on one operand

bug_categories.description: Change the wrap comparison from q == 999 to q == 1000 (or q == 998), so the counter wraps one count late or early.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a modulo-1000 counter (0-999). Altering the terminal constant changes the period to 1001 or 999 and breaks the expected count sequence.

bug_categories.description: Replace 999 with a nearby but incorrect value such as 99, 511, 1023 or 990, so the counter wraps at the wrong point.
bug_categories.applicability: The literal 999 is the sole definition of the modulus. A different constant keeps the code valid but yields a different period, for example a mod-100 counter.

bug_categories.description: Remove the reset term from the condition, giving if (q == 999), or invert it to !reset, so reset no longer clears the counter or clears it when it is deasserted.
bug_categories.applicability: The synchronous reset is ORed with the terminal-count check. Dropping or inverting it means q is never initialized or is held at 0 during normal operation.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset/wrap assignment from q <= 0 to q <= 1 (or another non-zero value), so the counter restarts from the wrong value.
bug_categories.applicability: Both reset and rollover share one q <= 0 assignment. A wrong value shifts the sequence start and shortens the wrap period to 999 counts.

bug_categories.description: Change q <= q + 1 to q <= q + 2, or to q <= q - 1, so the counter skips values or counts down.
bug_categories.applicability: With step 2 the counter reaches 998 then 1000 and never equals 999, so it runs past 999 up to the 10-bit limit instead of wrapping. Counting down wraps at the wrong point entirely.

bug_categories.description: Change reset || (q == 999) to reset && (q == 999), or use a bitwise | or & in place of ||.
bug_categories.applicability: With && the counter only clears when reset is asserted at the exact count 999, so reset is effectively ignored and the counter overflows past 999. This is a plausible slip in the combined reset/wrap condition.

bug_categories.description: Narrow the output from [9:0] to [8:0] or [7:0], so q cannot hold values up to 999.
bug_categories.applicability: 999 needs 10 bits. With a narrower q, the comparison q == 999 can never be true, since 999 is wider than q, and the counter wraps naturally at 512 or 256 instead of 1000.

bug_categories.description: Change the clock edge to negedge clk, use a blocking assignment (=), or add the reset to the sensitivity list as an asynchronous reset (posedge reset).
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on a synchronous reset with a nonblocking update on posedge clk. Changing the edge or making reset asynchronous alters the timing of the clear and the sampled value of q, which would show up in cycle-accurate comparisons.

bug_categories.bug_type: Asynchronous reset converted to synchronous reset
bug_categories.description: Remove 'or posedge areset' from the sensitivity list so the always block is only triggered by posedge clk, making the reset synchronous.
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on asynchronous reset behavior; areset asserted between clock edges would no longer clear q immediately, and a glitch or short pulse on areset could be missed entirely.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset condition from if(areset) to if(!areset) while leaving the posedge areset sensitivity, or change the edge to negedge areset, so the reset is active at the wrong level.
bug_categories.applicability: With the inverted condition, q is cleared during normal operation (areset=0) and passes data only while areset is high, completely breaking the register's function.

bug_categories.description: Change the reset assignment from q <= 0 to a non-zero constant such as q <= 8'hFF or q <= 8'h01.
bug_categories.applicability: The 8-bit output q is expected to be cleared to zero on reset. A different reset value yields wrong post-reset output and fails reset checks.

bug_categories.description: Reset only part of the register, e.g. q[3:0] <= 4'b0, leaving the upper bits holding their previous value on reset.
bug_categories.applicability: q is 8 bits wide; a partial reset leaves stale data in q[7:4] after areset, which is subtle and only caught when the upper bits are non-zero before reset.

bug_categories.description: Assign q from a permuted or reversed version of d, such as q <= {d[0],d[1],...,d[7]}, or swap the nibbles with q <= {d[3:0], d[7:4]}.
bug_categories.applicability: The data path is a straight 8-bit copy from d to q; bit reversal or nibble swap still compiles at the same width but corrupts the data.

bug_categories.description: Change the clock sensitivity from posedge clk to negedge clk.
bug_categories.applicability: The register should capture d on the rising edge of clk; sampling on the falling edge shifts capture timing by half a cycle and produces different output values against a posedge-based testbench.

bug_categories.bug_type: Blocking vs non-blocking assignment misuse or data corruption
bug_categories.description: Alter the data path so q is not a pure copy of d, e.g. q <= d + 1, q <= ~d, or q <= d & 8'hFE (stuck-at-zero LSB).
bug_categories.applicability: The module is a plain D register; any combinational modification of d before storing, including stuck bits or inversion, silently changes the output while remaining valid Verilog.

bug_categories.bug_type: Missing or conditional update (enable/hold logic error)
bug_categories.description: Add an unintended hold condition so q only updates when a condition holds, e.g. else if (d != 0) q <= d, or else if (q == 0) q <= d.
bug_categories.applicability: q must load d on every clock edge when not in reset; the added condition makes q retain stale values (e.g. d cannot return to 0), creating latch-like state-holding behavior.

mutants.bug_type: Blocking vs non-blocking assignment misuse or data corruption

bug_categories.description: Replace the XOR operator in the continuous assignment with another bitwise operator such as AND, OR, or XNOR.
bug_categories.applicability: out_assign = a ^ b becomes a & b, a | b, or ~(a ^ b), so the combinational output no longer computes the exclusive-or of the inputs.

bug_categories.description: Add an unintended inversion to one of the three outputs so it disagrees with the other two.
bug_categories.applicability: out_always_comb = ~(a ^ b) in the always @(*) block, so it is the complement of out_assign and out_always_ff for every input combination.

bug_categories.description: Replace the implicit @(*) sensitivity list with an explicit list that omits one of the inputs, creating a latch-like or stale-value simulation behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: always @(a) out_always_comb = a ^ b; means changes on b do not update out_always_comb, so it holds a stale value in simulation while out_assign updates correctly.

bug_categories.description: Change the assignment type in one of the procedural blocks, which alters scheduling and race behavior.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing out_always_ff <= a ^ b to out_always_ff = a ^ b in the clocked block, or changing out_always_comb = to <=, can introduce simulation race conditions and ordering differences relative to other logic sampling these signals.

bug_categories.description: Change the triggering edge of the sequential block so the register samples at a different time than intended.
bug_categories.applicability: always @(negedge clk) out_always_ff <= a ^ b; shifts the sampling to the falling edge, changing output timing relative to the clock, or using @(posedge clk or negedge clk) makes it update twice per cycle.

bug_categories.description: Use the same input twice or replace one input with a constant in one of the expressions.
bug_categories.applicability: out_always_ff <= a ^ a (always 0) or a ^ 1'b0 (just a), so the registered output ignores b and stops reflecting the XOR of the inputs.

bug_categories.bug_type: Extra pipeline delay or missing register stage
bug_categories.description: Change the timing relationship by adding an intermediate register or by removing the register from the sequential path.
bug_categories.applicability: Introducing an intermediate reg stage so out_always_ff reflects a ^ b delayed by two clock cycles, or converting out_always_ff into a combinational assign so it no longer lags by one clock cycle.

bug_categories.description: Add flawed reset or enable conditions to the sequential block that gate or force the output value incorrectly.
bug_categories.applicability: Adding a condition such as if (a) out_always_ff <= a ^ b; or forcing out_always_ff <= 1'b1 under some condition makes the flop fail to update on every clock edge, so it holds old values or outputs a wrong constant.

bug_categories.description: Swap the mux select in the fan expression so that mode=1 selects too_hot and mode=0 selects too_cold, i.e. ((mode)? too_hot : too_cold) | fan_on.
bug_categories.applicability: The fan output uses a ternary operator on 'mode' to choose between too_cold (heating) and too_hot (cooling). Swapping the branches makes the fan respond to the wrong temperature condition in each mode.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND in the heater assignment with OR: heater = mode | too_cold.
bug_categories.applicability: The heater should only be on when in heating mode AND too cold. Using OR turns the heater on whenever mode is 1 or the room is too cold, including in cooling mode.

bug_categories.description: Remove the negation of mode in the aircon assignment: aircon = mode & too_hot.
bug_categories.applicability: The aircon is supposed to be active in cooling mode (mode=0). Dropping the '~' makes it active in heating mode and inactive in cooling mode, and it can be on simultaneously with the heater when both too_cold and too_hot are asserted.

bug_categories.description: Use the wrong temperature input in an assignment, e.g. heater = mode & too_hot or aircon = ~mode & too_cold.
bug_categories.applicability: The module has two similar temperature inputs (too_cold, too_hot). Mixing them up in heater or aircon produces plausible-looking but functionally wrong behavior, such as heating when too hot.

bug_categories.description: Change the OR with fan_on to AND: fan = ((mode)? too_cold : too_hot) & fan_on.
bug_categories.applicability: fan_on is a manual override that should force the fan on regardless of temperature. Using AND makes the fan run only when both the manual override and the temperature condition hold, so the override no longer works alone.

bug_categories.description: Remove the '| fan_on' term so fan depends only on the mode-selected temperature condition.
bug_categories.applicability: The fan output is the OR of automatic demand and manual fan_on. Removing it leaves the fan_on input unused and the manual fan control non-functional.

bug_categories.description: Alter grouping so fan_on binds into only one branch of the mux, e.g. fan = (mode) ? too_cold : (too_hot | fan_on), or drop the parentheses around the ternary.
bug_categories.applicability: The fan expression combines a ternary with a bitwise OR. Moving fan_on inside one branch means the manual override only works in cooling mode (mode=0) and is ignored in heating mode.

bug_categories.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical / negation of output
bug_categories.description: Invert or alter the final polarity of an output, e.g. assign aircon = ~(~mode & too_hot), or heater = ~(mode & too_cold) (NAND).
bug_categories.applicability: The outputs are simple active-high combinational functions. Adding an inversion makes heater or aircon active-low, so they are asserted when there is no demand and deasserted when there is.

mutants.bug_type: Bitwise vs logical / negation of output

bug_categories.description: Remove the outer inversion so z = x ^ y, turning the XNOR into an XOR and inverting the output for every input combination.
bug_categories.applicability: The design is a single XNOR expression ~(x ^ y). Dropping the ~ operator is a trivial, syntactically valid change that completely inverts the function.

bug_categories.description: Replace the inner XOR with a bitwise AND, giving z = ~(x & y), which is a NAND gate.
bug_categories.applicability: Replacing ^ with & inside the parentheses yields valid Verilog. The output matches XNOR only for some inputs (e.g., 00 gives 1 in both, but 11 gives 0 instead of 1).

bug_categories.description: Replace the inner XOR with a bitwise OR, giving z = ~(x | y), which is a NOR gate.
bug_categories.applicability: Swapping ^ for | produces a valid expression. The output is 1 only when both inputs are 0, so the case x=y=1 incorrectly yields 0.

bug_categories.description: Replace the bitwise inversion ~ with the logical negation !, or the bitwise ^ with a logical comparison like !=, producing z = !(x ^ y) or z = ~(x != y). Results can differ in semantics on wider or X/Z-valued signals.
bug_categories.applicability: Because x, y, z are single-bit, results are mostly equivalent for 0/1 values, but a variant such as z = (x != y) (dropping the inversion by using a logical inequality) breaks XNOR behavior and tests whether verification catches subtle operator-class changes.

bug_categories.description: Use the same signal for both operands, e.g., z = ~(x ^ x) or z = ~(y ^ y), so the output becomes a constant 1 independent of the other input.
bug_categories.applicability: With only two inputs, replacing one operand with the other makes one input unused and z stuck at 1, which a testbench must detect by toggling both inputs independently.

bug_categories.description: Move the inversion onto only one operand, e.g., z = (~x) ^ y or x ^ (~y) -- this is logically equivalent to XNOR, so instead apply it incorrectly, such as z = ~x ^ ~y, which equals x ^ y (double inversion cancels) and thus behaves as XOR.
bug_categories.applicability: Changing the placement or count of ~ operators gives plausible-looking code. z = ~x ^ ~y silently becomes XOR, a realistic precedence/negation mistake that differs from the specification.

bug_categories.description: Replace the logic expression with a constant, such as assign z = 1'b1 or 1'b0, or tie z to only one input (z = x).
bug_categories.applicability: The single continuous assignment can be replaced with a constant or pass-through of one input, simulating a stuck-at fault or lost logic, which only fails for a subset of input combinations that a thorough test must cover.

bug_categories.description: Implement the function as a conditional that is correct for three input combinations but wrong for one, e.g., z = (x & y) | (~x & ~y & ~y) replaced with z = (x & y) | (~x & y), giving wrong output at x=0,y=0.
bug_categories.applicability: XNOR has a four-row truth table; rewriting it as a sum-of-products with a missing or incorrect minterm creates a corner-case bug (such as wrong output when both inputs are 0) that exhaustive input testing must reveal.

bug_categories.description: Replace the AND operator in the out_both assignment with OR, so out_both[2:0] = in[2:0] | in[3:1].
bug_categories.applicability: out_both[2:0] is meant to flag adjacent bits that are both 1. Using OR makes it behave like out_any and gives wrong results whenever only one of the two neighbors is high.

bug_categories.description: Replace the OR operator in the out_any assignment with AND, so out_any[3:1] = in[2:0] & in[3:1].
bug_categories.applicability: out_any[3:1] should be set when either neighbor is 1. With AND it only asserts when both neighbors are 1, making it identical to out_both for those bits.

bug_categories.description: Change out_different to use XNOR (~^) instead of XOR, inverting every bit of the result.
bug_categories.applicability: out_different = in ^ {in[0], in[3:1]} detects differing neighbors. XNOR flips it to detect equal neighbors, so every output bit is inverted.

bug_categories.description: Shift the slice on one operand of out_both or out_any, e.g. in[2:0] & in[3:1] becomes in[3:1] & in[3:1] or in[2:0] & in[2:0].
bug_categories.applicability: The design relies on pairing each bit with its neighbor via the offset slices [2:0] and [3:1]. A wrong offset makes the operation compare a bit with itself or the wrong neighbor, so the neighbor-detection logic is lost.

bug_categories.description: Alter the concatenation in out_different, e.g. use {in[3], in[3:1]} or {in[0], in[2:0]} instead of {in[0], in[3:1]}.
bug_categories.applicability: The concatenation implements a circular right rotation so that the top bit is compared with in[0]. A wrong MSB or wrong slice breaks the wrap-around comparison for in[3] and possibly other bits.

bug_categories.description: Misalign the output slice with the input slices, e.g. out_both[3:1] = in[2:0] & in[3:1] or out_any[2:0] = in[2:0] | in[3:1].
bug_categories.applicability: Each output bit i must correspond to the pair (in[i], in[i+1]) for out_both and (in[i-1], in[i]) for out_any. Shifting the destination slice moves results to the wrong output bit positions, leaving different bits undriven.

bug_categories.bug_type: Don't-care (x) replaced with constant or logic value
bug_categories.description: Replace the 1'bx assignments for out_both[3] and out_any[0] with defined constants (0 or 1) or with real logic such as in[3] & in[0] and in[3] | in[0].
bug_categories.applicability: out_both[3] and out_any[0] are unspecified outputs that the spec treats as don't care. Driving them with defined values changes the output behavior and can mismatch a reference that expects x, and a wrong logic function there would be a functional bug.

bug_categories.bug_type: Missing or duplicate bit drivers (incomplete assignment)
bug_categories.description: Remove one of the partial assignments (for example the out_both[3] or out_any[0] line), or change a slice range so bits are left undriven or driven by two assignments.
bug_categories.applicability: out_both and out_any are each built from two separate assigns covering disjoint slices. Dropping or overlapping one leaves a bit as high-impedance/undriven (z) or creates multiple drivers resolving to x, which breaks the output relative to the specification.

bug_categories.bug_type: Incorrect constant value in case arm
bug_categories.description: Change the output value assigned for one of the input patterns so the lowest-set-bit position is wrong for that input.
bug_categories.applicability: In the case statement, e.g. 4'h4 assigns 2'h2 but could be changed to 2'h1 or 2'h3, or 4'h8 assigns 2'h3 but could be changed to 2'h2. This yields a wrong priority-encoder output for a single input.

bug_categories.description: Exchange the output values between two case items so that two inputs produce each other's expected result.
bug_categories.applicability: Swap the outputs of 4'h4 (2'h2) and 4'h8 (2'h3), or of 4'h2 (2'h1) and 4'hc (2'h2). Both remain valid Verilog but break the lowest-set-bit encoding.

bug_categories.description: Make an odd input (bit 0 set) return a nonzero position instead of 0, breaking the rule that bit 0 has the highest priority and maps to position 0.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 4'h1, 4'h3, 4'h5, 4'h7, 4'h9, 4'hb, 4'hd or 4'hf to assign 2'h1 or another nonzero value, so the encoder reports a wrong position when bit 0 is set along with other bits.

bug_categories.description: Reverse the priority direction so the highest set bit wins instead of the lowest for multi-bit inputs.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 4'h6 (2'h1) to 2'h2, 4'hc (2'h2) to 2'h3, 4'hf (2'h0) to 2'h3, and similar entries, so inputs with multiple set bits resolve to the MSB position.

bug_categories.description: Remove one case arm so the input falls through to the default assignment, which outputs 0.
bug_categories.applicability: Delete 4'hc, 4'he or 4'h8. Their outputs become 2'b0 through the default branch and are wrong (2'h2, 2'h1, and 2'h3 expected). Valid Verilog, but silently incorrect.

bug_categories.description: Change the default assignment, or the value for input 0, to something nonzero, altering behavior for the no-bit-set case and for any arms that are removed or unmatched.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 4'h0: pos = 2'h0 to 2'h3, or change default: pos = 2'b0 to 2'b11. The input-zero case and the default case then diverge from the reference design.

bug_categories.description: Change a case label to duplicate another, so the first match takes precedence and the intended arm becomes unreachable.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 4'hc to 4'h8, or 4'ha to 4'h2. The input that lost its arm falls to default (0) while the duplicate label is shadowed, so wrong outputs appear for specific inputs.

bug_categories.description: Alter a case label (a wrong hex digit or width) so the output is assigned to the wrong input pattern.
bug_categories.applicability: Change 4'h6 to 4'h9 or 4'he to 4'h7. The intended input then loses its mapping and the wrong input gets that output, which shows up as incorrect pos for exactly two input patterns.

mutants.bug_type: Incorrect constant value in case arm
